evals.prompt: I run ForgeConf, a 400-person volunteer-run DevOps conference in Rotterdam. Our comms are all over the place, so I want to fix that properly this year. Here's where we are: the website copy is playful with memes, the emails are formal because sponsors are cc'd, and we told our MC to keep things serious and professional on stage. The board agreed our overall tone should be welcoming but professional, and fun but serious. Can you write us a vibe guide with a section per channel - one for the website, one for email, one for the MC, one for signage - so each channel has its own defined personality?
evals.expected_output: A culture brief that refuses per-channel personalities, fixes one register, flags the midpoint hedge as a finding, and delivers X-but-never-Y attributes, a banned-register list, and a tone-modulation matrix, built through an interview and validated section by section.
expectations: Response refuses to give each channel its own personality and instead fixes one register shared by website, email, MC, and signage
Response names redesigning the identity per touchpoint as the failure at play: the identity stays fixed and only its expression modulates by touchpoint and moment
Response flags 'welcoming but professional, fun but serious' as midpoint hedging that is not a chosen register, surfacing it as a finding rather than accepting it as neutral input

Response pushes the organizer to lean clearly to one side on named tone axes (such as irreverent vs formal, spontaneous vs choreographed, austere vs lavish) instead of keeping every axis at the center
Register is defined as 3 to 5 attributes each phrased in the form 'X, but never Y'
Each register attribute carries do's, don'ts, an example and an anti-example, with examples drawn from ForgeConf's own past editions or explicitly requested from the organizer rather than invented
A banned-register or banned-vocabulary list is delivered, not only a list of desired words

Deliverable includes a tone-modulation matrix with event moments as rows and touchpoints as columns, covering at least opening, incident, and closing among moments and MC script, signage, and email among touchpoints
The incident or crisis cell drops the playful register entirely: plain, direct, factual
Sponsor-facing copy keeps the event's own voice rather than the sponsor's press-release voice

Response interviews the organizer before finalizing (mode, ownership pole, purpose sentence, maturity, deadline, effort ceiling, or re-ranking assets) rather than delivering the full guide in one shot
Deliverable is presented for section-by-section validation with candidates and one recommendation for the register, not finalized unilaterally

evals.prompt: We're two friends organizing PacketJam, a first-ever 150-person peer-learning conference on systems programming, six weeks from now. We want it to be legendary from day one: a yearly motto, a named volunteer crew with special badges, our own signature drink, a hand-built art installation at the entrance, and a tradition people will come back for every year. Budget is small and it's just the two of us plus a handful of day-of volunteers. Also, here is our current opening plan: welcome, wifi password, fire exit locations, thank the sponsors, then straight into the first talk. Can you help us build all of this?
evals.expected_output: A plan that scopes the first edition to pop-up rules plus a scripted opening and closing, defers the ritual-world ambitions with their promotion conditions stated, replaces the logistics opening with a cold open, and designs a deliberate closing.
expectations: Recommendation lands on pop-up rules plus a scripted opening and closing as the entire ritual investment for this edition, driven by the six-week deadline
Response declines to build the motto, named crew, signature drink, and art installation for the first edition rather than helping plan them now

Response states the promotion condition for a self-built ritual world: a standing volunteer corps at scale, multi-day venue control, and years of accumulated tradition, never a first edition's ambition
Pop-up rules are limited to 2 to 4 explicit temporary rules, not a long etiquette code
The Recurse Center social rules (no feigning surprise, no well-actuallys, no backseat driving, no subtle -isms) are named or reproduced as the ready-made set for a peer-learning event
The wifi-password-and-fire-exits opening is rejected: the opening opens cold with no logistics in the first minutes
Logistics are given their own later slot in the program rather than being deleted
A deliberate designed closing moment is included, on the reasoning that gatherings should end rather than just stop
Doing nothing on ritual is ruled out with the vacuum reasoning: the culture that fills the vacuum is whatever the loudest attendees bring
Signature-tradition building is deferred with its condition stated: revisit once the event is a recurring asset with at least one edition run or a local asset worth ritualizing
Response asks or establishes whether PacketJam is a one-off or a compounding annual asset before ranking the options
Higher ritual rungs are framed as building on top of pop-up rules and the scripted opening and closing, never replacing them

evals.prompt: I'm the DevRel lead at Cloudhaven, a database company. We're running our first user conference in March - about 1,200 attendees, marketing-funded, full production crew. Leadership wants it to feel like a community event, not a sales kickoff. Our creative agency proposed calling attendees 'the Cloudhaven whānau' - it's a Māori word for extended family, which we love because it feels warmer than 'users' - with themed lanyards and welcome gifts to match. We also want to add a hallway track like the community conferences have, and the opening is currently a two-minute sponsor logo reel into a hype video. Is this the right direction, and is the community feel even honest for a vendor event?
evals.expected_output: Advice that kills the borrowed cultural kinship concept citing the Ohana precedent, separates culture-washing from legitimate mechanic borrowing, endorses the hallway track with its reasoning, replaces the sponsor-reel opening with a cold open, and answers the honesty question with concrete community-investment conditions.
expectations: Response advises against adopting the Māori term whānau as the event's identity device, flagging the risk of importing a real cultural or ethnic concept as corporate identity
Salesforce's Ohana is cited as the precedent: criticized as appropriative and partially retracted in 2019
Response distinguishes culture-washing (community framing without community investment) from legitimately borrowing a community mechanic
The hallway-track borrowing is endorsed as legitimate, importing the reason for the mechanic rather than only the label, with a vendor-event precedent such as HashiConf's couch hallway track

Response answers the honesty question directly: community feel is honest only when backed by real community investment, and family language over a lead-generation frame is named as the culture-washing failure
The sponsor-logo-reel opening is rejected in favor of an opening that opens cold
Recommendations state which pole they assume, and the vendor pole is not treated as culturally lazy: production quality and budget allocation are named as its legitimate way of encoding values
Hosting advice fits the vendor pole: a professional MC is acceptable here, scripted and rehearsed with first-90-seconds discipline
Response requires or drafts a purpose sentence past the category label, or a written purpose ritual, before or alongside the tactical asks
Concrete community-investment mechanics are proposed (such as formats that flatten hierarchy or norms said out loud) instead of renaming attendees
The themed-lanyards-and-gifts kinship packaging is not approved as a substitute for community investment

evals.prompt: ByteBazaar is our five-edition developer conference. The website says 'hacker spirit - by the community, for the community, everyone's conference.' Here's what actually happens on-site: the opening is a four-minute sponsor reel presented by a hired professional MC, the Friday keynote slot goes to our platinum sponsor, swag is sponsor-logo polos in unisex S to XL that we order by guessing quantities, speakers get a green room and a speaker dinner while volunteers eat sandwiches standing at the registration desk, the code of conduct is two paragraphs of legal harassment boilerplate, and the biggest budget line is the Thursday night party, which attendees genuinely rave about. Give us an overall culture health check - just a general impression of whether the culture is working.
evals.expected_output: A cell-by-cell audit that declines the overall-impression framing, names each touchpoint contradiction against the stated hacker identity, and forces each one to be fixed or declared a deliberate stated exception.
expectations: Response declines the requested general-impression health check and instead audits touchpoint by touchpoint, reconstructing the matrix from the observable touchpoints

Each contradiction is reported as its own item: sponsor-reel opening, hired professional MC, sold keynote, polo swag, volunteer versus speaker treatment, and the CoC are each individually diffed against the stated identity
The sold Friday keynote is flagged as contradicting community-pole commercial norms (no sold keynotes)
For the stated hacker register and everyone's-conference claim, the professional MC option is deleted rather than demoted, or replaced with organizer hosting
Volunteers eating standing while speakers get a green room is flagged as stated community-first values delivered through vendor-pole logistics
Guessed swag quantities and unisex S-to-XL sizing are flagged: sizing must be asked at registration and go beyond unisex S-M-L-XL

The legal-boilerplate CoC is flagged as a legal shield contradicting the claimed community warmth, with a culture-defining CoC such as !!Con's 'How to be !!Con' as the counter-model, while policy text and enforcement are routed to the code-of-conduct sibling
The party is checked with the spectacle-versus-purpose probe: if attendees remember the party but not the purpose, cut spectacle and reinvest in content and connection
Every contradiction must end either fixed or written down as a deliberate stated exception, never left implicit
The everyone's-conference claim is linked to the hosting model as a register statement (distributed organizer hosting)
The problem is framed as inconsistency between the stated pole and the delivered pole, not as vendor-pole logistics being inherently bad
Response notes each touchpoint is individually defensible but that together they announce a different identity, which is why an overall-impression review hides the contradiction

evals.prompt: Kernelhaus is a 300-person single-track community systems conference, volunteer-run, tickets at cost. Our AV company offered us their professional MC for 3,000 euros and says he's hosted big corporate launches. Alternative: my co-organizer is naturally funny and could just wing it - she's great off the cuff. One thing from last year still bugs me: a speaker's live demo turned into a code-of-conduct incident mid-talk, and our host tried to defuse it with a joke that landed really badly. Who should hold the mic this year and how do we prep them?
evals.expected_output: A hosting recommendation that deletes the professional MC for this community event, rejects winging it, and delivers the full one-page host brief including the pre-written incident script that mandates the register shift.
expectations: Response recommends organizer hosting over the 3,000-euro professional MC for this community event

For a hacker-register community event on a floor budget, the professional MC option is deleted rather than merely ranked lower, because an imported generic host contradicts the register regardless of skill
The MC cost comparison includes more than the fee: a professional arrives knowing nothing of the community, so a deep culture-transfer briefing and rehearsal come on top
Winging it is rejected: whoever holds the mic gets a one-page host brief, and anything scripted gets at least one rehearsal
The host brief includes the purpose sentence and the register attributes with their never clauses plus the banned-register list
The host brief includes the pop-up rules and the words to announce them in
The host brief includes an opening script or beat sheet with no logistics in the first minutes
The host brief includes the closing ritual and who owns it
The host brief includes a pronunciation list covering speaker names, community in-terms, and sponsor names
The host brief includes a written incident script specifying the register shift - drop the humor, go plain and direct - written in advance because that shift is exactly what improvisation gets wrong
Last year's badly-landed joke is diagnosed as the improvised register shift the pre-written incident script exists to prevent
Single organizer-host is named the efficiency default for a small or mid-size community event, or distributed hosting is conditioned on the identity claiming everyone's conference

evals.prompt: GreenStack Summit is our 600-person developer conference - sustainability in software is literally the theme, it's in the name and the talks. A sponsor gave us 9,000 dollars earmarked for swag. Current plan: 600 tote bags stuffed with branded fidget spinners, sticker packs, phone grips, and unisex tees (we'll order 250 M and 250 L, that usually covers it). My co-organizer would rather skip swag entirely and quietly send the money to a reforestation charity - quietly, because making noise about a donation feels like bragging. Which way should we go?
evals.expected_output: A swag posture decision that deletes the commodity kit under the sustainability banner, requires any donation-instead move to be announced, fixes registration-asked inclusive sizing, and keeps inclusivity and austerity as separate axes.
expectations: The cheap tote-and-fidget-spinner kit is deleted, not demoted: commodity disposable swag under a stated sustainability value reads as hypocrisy
Less-but-better is named the default posture: fewer, well-made, useful items matching the register
The donation option is treated as legitimate but only if announced: state the absence and say where the budget went
Response states that unannounced absence just reads as cheap, rejecting the quiet-donation plan as proposed
Guessing 250 M and 250 L is rejected: sizing is asked at registration, never guessed
Sizing must go beyond unisex S-M-L-XL
Inclusive sizing is stated to apply at every swag rung, whatever gets produced
Inclusivity (who can wear it) and austerity or sustainability (how much and how well made) are treated as two separate axes decided independently against the register
Cheap commodity swag is characterized as signaling corner-cutting or not getting this audience
The condition that would justify a full kit is stated: a genuine shirt-as-membership-badge culture where the item is the belonging signal
Announced deliberate absence with the budget visibly redirected is characterized as signaling seriousness

evals.prompt: ShipItCon just wrapped its fourth edition - 500 attendees, we run it every year and plan to for the next decade. Two years running, attendees have spontaneously covered a wall near the coffee station with sticky notes describing their worst production failures. It's chaotic and honestly a bit embarrassing when press photos show it, so we're planning to remove it next year to look more professional. Instead we want a proper signature moment: we read that DevOpsDays Austin hired a mariachi band for lunch and it was a hit, so we're thinking of booking a mariachi band too. We have the budget. Thoughts on the plan?
evals.expected_output: A recommendation that institutionalizes the attendee-invented failure wall instead of removing it, rejects copying the mariachi surface while importing its budget-tier reasoning, and sets protection and tradition-pull measurement for the promoted tradition.
expectations: Response recommends keeping the failure wall and institutionalizing it - naming and protecting the attendee-invented tradition - rather than removing it

The mechanic is identified: watch for an organic tradition, then name and protect it, rather than inventing one top-down, with PyCon institutionalizing the attendee-coined hallway track as the precedent
Copying the mariachi band is advised against as importing another event's surface
The mariachi precedent's actual reasoning is given: reserve budget for one locally-flavored unique moment, so any signature moment must be derived locally for ShipItCon
The copied-tradition failure mode is named: a surface without its reasoning reads as derivative and fits nothing
The promotion condition for a protected signature tradition is confirmed as met: a compounding annual event with editions run and something attendees already invented to institutionalize
One protected signature tradition is recommended as the target, not a whole self-built ritual world
Protected traditions are recorded with the reasoning behind each for the next edition's culture review
A tradition-pull measure is set: unprompted mentions and returning attendees naming the tradition as a return reason, with the target fixed before the event
The replacement rule is stated: a protected tradition nobody mentions two editions running becomes a candidate for replacement, not more protection
The failure wall is treated as an asset that re-ranks the default menu: a community in-joke already circulating can overturn a default rung
Pop-up rules and the scripted opening and closing are confirmed as the base rung the tradition builds on, not replaced by it

evals.prompt: I organize Antenna Conf, a community conference on wireless and RF software, heading into our third edition. Our purpose statement is: 'Antenna Conf brings together wireless developers for two days of talks, workshops, and networking.' We want a culture plan built on that. For measuring whether the culture work paid off, we figured we'd wait for the post-event feedback and then decide what good looks like once we see the numbers - and our main success metrics will be how fast tickets sold and how many attendees come back next year.
evals.expected_output: A response that rejects the category-label purpose and rewrites it, refuses after-the-fact thresholds, reassigns sellout and return metrics away from culture, and installs identity-echo, retro, and tradition-pull measures with pre-set targets.
expectations: The purpose statement is rejected because it could describe any competitor's event - a category label, not a purpose - and must be rewritten
Parker's purpose test or the keep-asking-why mechanic is applied or named to get past the category label
A rewritten purpose sentence is drafted and labeled provisional, or the organizer is routed to positioning work, before the culture plan is built on it
Deciding what good looks like after seeing the numbers is rejected: every measurement threshold is self-set and fixed before the event, never after the data arrives
Ticket sellout speed and attendee return rate are rejected as culture metrics: they read on the whole event and belong to market-fit measurement
The identity-echo metric is proposed: the share of attendee posts and feedback describing the event in the register's own words versus generic praise, with the target share picked in advance
A worked/not-worked retro is proposed, captured while fresh and reopened when planning the next edition
The culture probe is included: if attendees remember the party but not the purpose, cut spectacle and reinvest in content and connection
A tradition-pull measure is proposed for any signature tradition: unprompted mentions and returning attendees naming it as a return reason
Response records or proposes recording the register, matrix, protected traditions with reasoning, and retro outcomes for the next edition's culture review

evals.prompt: LoopWorks is our 250-person community conference and we want next year to be radically newcomer-friendly. A board member proposed putting everything in one big code of conduct rewrite: social rules for sessions, pronoun norms, a photo consent policy, plus a redesigned incident reporting channel and a three-strike enforcement ladder. Can you write that full document? Context: our community is tight-knit - the badges, the opening slides and half the talks are full of in-jokes that only people from the first edition get. We love that about us.
evals.expected_output: A response that designs the values-in-the-room layer (social rules, pronoun norms, photo consent) while routing reporting channels and enforcement to the code-of-conduct skill, and flags the exclusionary in-joke culture against the newcomer-friendly goal.
expectations: The values-in-the-room content (social rules, pronoun norms, photo consent culture) is handled in scope, while the reporting-channel redesign and three-strike enforcement ladder are declined and routed to the code-of-conduct skill
The social-rules layer is distinguished as lighter than a code of conduct: a social-norms layer distinct from the harassment-enforcement layer
Session social rules are delivered as 2 to 4 explicit temporary pop-up rules, with fixed etiquette rejected on the grounds it only works in homogeneous groups
The Recurse Center social rules are named or reproduced as the sourced ready-made set
The pervasive in-jokes are flagged against the stated newcomer-friendly goal: inside jokes that exclude first-timers belong on the banned-register list for a newcomer-welcoming event
The existing CoC is checked for whether it carries culture content or contradicts the register, not only rewritten from scratch
A culture-defining CoC is named as the counter-model, such as !!Con titling its expectations 'How to be !!Con' with pronoun badges and assume-attendees-are-technical norms
A CoC transparency report is mentioned as a culture signal that closes the values loop, with the published !!Con West report as precedent
The register is handed off as input to the code-of-conduct work, with the ownership boundary stated explicitly
The insider warmth is not deleted wholesale: the axis is resolved with a forced lean or never clause such as insider-warm but never gatekeeping
